112679.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse fendinn (“the Devil”), probably from Old Frisian fandiand (“tempter”), the present participle of fandia (“to tempt”), from Proto-Germanic *fandōną (“to seek, search for, examine”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pent- (“to pass; path”).
Alternatively, the late Old Norse form may have developed from or been influenced by older fjándi (“enemy; devil”), definite fjándinn. On this analysis, compare *fijandz (“enemy, fiend”), the present participle of *fijāną (“to hate”), ultimately from *peh₁- (“to hate, hurt”). The two formations may have influenced one another.

61223.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse tjóðra (“to tether”), a denominal verb formed from tjóðr (“tether”) with the verb-forming suffix -a. The noun is from Proto-Germanic *teudrą (“tether; cord, rope”), also reconstructed as *tūdrą. By surface analysis, tjor (“tether”) + e (“verb-forming suffix”).
The further origin of the Proto-Germanic noun is uncertain. It has been connected with *dewk- (“to pull”) or *dewh₂- (“to tie, secure”), with an instrumental noun suffix, while another proposal connects it with *deh₁-. Doublet of tøyre (“to tether, restrain”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk tjore and tjora, Danish tøj

1000487.etyen:
A spelling variant of Jon, ultimately a short form of Johannes, from Ancient Greek Ἰωάννης (Iōánnēs), from Biblical Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (Yōḥānān, “Yahweh is gracious”). The spelling with ⟨h⟩ was already common in Norway during the 18th century, before substantial English influence on Norwegian naming practices, although later use may also have been reinforced by English John. The surname is derived from the corresponding given name.
Compare Danish John, Swedish John and English John (“male given name”).

x: Vi skal ha tacofredag i dag, har du lyst å komme?
We are having Taco Friday today; would you like to come?
Ingrid Alexandra beskriver en familiehverdag som mange kan kjenne seg igjen i. Sangkonkurranse på TV, brettspill og tacofredager.
Ingrid Alexandra describes a family life that many can recognize: singing competitions on television, board games, and Taco Fridays.

1004839.etyen:
From taco (“taco”) + fredag (“Friday”), literally “Taco Friday”, referring to a Friday evening or recurring Friday occasion centred on eating taco. The first element, taco, is borrowed from Spanish taco (“taco; plug, block”). The second element, fredag, is inherited from Old Norse frjádagr (“Friday”), from Proto-West Germanic *Frījā dag (“day of Frigg”), a Germanic calque of Latin dies Veneris (“day of Venus”). The compound is first attested in 2006.
Compare the equivalent Swedish formation tacofredag and Finnish tacoperjantai (“Taco Friday”).

1005095.etyen:
From evangelisere (“to evangelize”) + -ing (“action/result-forming noun suffix”).
The base verb, evangelisere (“to evangelize”), is from Late Latin ēvangelizāre (“to preach the Gospel”), the present active infinitive of ēvangelizō (“to preach the Gospel”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek εὐαγγελίζω (euangelízō, “to bring good news; to preach the Gospel”). The Greek verb is formed from εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion, “good news, gospel”) and -ίζω (-ízō, “verb-forming suffix”).
